Spectroscopy. The study of the interaction between electromagnetic radiation and matter. By measuring the absorption, emission, or scattering of light across different wavelengths, chemists can identify the structure, composition, and physical properties of chemical compounds. It encompasses a wide range of methods, from simple colorimetry to complex multi-dimensional resonance techniques.

The fundamental principle in spectroscopy is the Beer-Lambert law for liquid solutions, which states that absorbance is directly proportional to the concentration of the analyte, the path length of the sample cell, and the molar attenuation coefficient. Different spectroscopic methods probe different properties of matter. Nuclear magnetic resonance, or NMR, spectroscopy maps the carbon-hydrogen framework of organic compounds, exploiting the spin states of nuclei in a strong magnetic field. Carbon-thirteen NMR spectroscopy is a fundamental tool for determining the skeletal structures of organic carbon molecules.

Infrared spectroscopy identifies functional groups by measuring the absorption of infrared light as it excites specific molecular bonds to stretch, bend, or vibrate. Ultraviolet-visible, or UV-Vis, spectroscopy observes electronic transitions of valence electrons and is commonly used to study conjugated carbon systems and transition metal complexes. Helium itself was first discovered in eighteen sixty-eight through solar emission spectroscopy during a solar eclipse before it was ever isolated on Earth. Sodium emission spectroscopy produces the characteristic yellow doublet D-lines that are distinctive in the sodium vapor spectrum.

Spectroscopy is also coupled with other analytical techniques. Gas Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry, or GC-MS, joins chromatography with spectroscopy, although mass spectrometry itself measures mass-to-charge ratios of ionized fragments rather than light absorption.
